name: Zechariah
author: Zechariah was a prophet, a man who brought messages he believed came from God. He was the son of Berechiah and grandson of Iddo, and he likely came from a priestly family that had returned from exile in Babylon. He worked alongside the prophet Haggai, beginning around 520 BC. Chapters 1–8 are widely accepted as his, but many scholars think chapters 9–14 come from a later writer or writers, while others hold that Zechariah wrote the whole book.
audience: The first hearers were Jews who had come back to Jerusalem and Judah after about seventy years of exile in Babylon. They lived in a small, poor community among ruins, and their work rebuilding God's temple had stalled for years amid hardship, opposition and discouragement.
era: The Persian Empire ruled the region after defeating Babylon, and in 538 BC the Persian king Cyrus allowed exiled Jews to return home. Foundations for a new temple were laid, but work stopped for nearly two decades. King Darius I took the throne in 522 BC after a period of revolts across the empire, and under the encouragement of Haggai and Zechariah the temple was finally completed around 516 BC.

notes.1:1: Dated to the eighth month of Darius's second year, around October or November 520 BC, shortly after Haggai began urging the people to rebuild.
notes.1:7: Dated to the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, around February 519 BC; this opens a series of eight visions Zechariah saw in a single night.
notes.2:6: Part of this section is addressed to Jews who were still living in Babylon rather than returning to Jerusalem.
notes.3:1: Joshua was the high priest, the chief religious leader of the returned community and the first to hold that office after the exile.
notes.4:1: Zerubbabel was the Persian-appointed governor of Judah, a descendant of King David, and he led the work of rebuilding the temple.
notes.6:9: Three men, Heldai, Tobijah and Jedaiah, had just arrived from the exiles in Babylon bringing gifts of silver and gold.
notes.7:1: Dated to late 518 BC, when a delegation, probably sent from the town of Bethel, asked whether the people should keep fasting to mourn the temple's destruction by Babylon in 586 BC.
notes.8:18: The four fasts mentioned recalled sad events around Jerusalem's fall: the siege, the city walls breached, the temple burned, and the murder of governor Gedaliah.
notes.9:1: Names cities of Syria, Phoenicia and Philistia; some scholars connect this with Alexander the Great's march down that coast in 332 BC.
notes.9:11: This passage mentions Greece, one reason some scholars date these later chapters to a time when Greek power was rising.
notes.12:10: It refers to mourning at Hadad-rimmon near Megiddo, often linked to the grief after good King Josiah was killed in battle there in 609 BC.
notes.14:1: It recalls an earthquake in the days of King Uzziah of Judah, around 760 BC, which Israel remembered for centuries afterward.
notes.14:16: The Feast of Tabernacles, or Booths, was an autumn harvest festival when Israelites lived in temporary shelters, remembering their wilderness journey after leaving Egypt.

flags.problem: "About seventy years of exile" is doubtful as a historical figure. Seventy years is the traditional prophetic number, which Zechariah himself uses. But Jerusalem fell in 586 BC and the first return came in 538 BC, which is under fifty years. Many of the returnees had been born in Babylon.
flags.suggestion: Write "after decades of exile in Babylon" or "after about fifty years of exile in Babylon". Or note that seventy years was the traditional reckoning.

flags.problem: The mention of Greece is in 9:13, not 9:11. Verse 9:11 is about something else, so a reader tapping this note will not find what it describes.
The mourning at Hadad-rimmon near Megiddo is in 12:11, not 12:10. Verse 12:10 is a well-known verse on a different subject, so attaching this note to it could confuse readers.
The earthquake in the days of King Uzziah is mentioned in 14:5, not 14:1. Verse 14:1 does not mention it, so "It recalls an earthquake" is wrong for that verse.
